hops.afterHeading: Two processes decide when you sleep
hops.title: Why going to bed early can be surprisingly hard
hops.text: Try turning in two hours early before a dawn flight and you may well lie there wide awake. In 1986 the sleep researcher Peretz Lavie kept volunteers up all night, then cycled them around the clock: 13 minutes awake, then 7 minutes in bed trying to sleep. Exhausted, they had the hardest time falling asleep between roughly 8 and 10 PM, a window Lavie called the "forbidden zone" for sleep. Later, sleep came on abruptly, all at once, at what he called the "sleep gate." In the lesson's model, the clock holds the upper level high in the evening, so climbing pressure has a hard time reaching it.

sources.citation: Lavie P, Electroencephalography and Clinical Neurophysiology 63(5):414-425 (1986).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A young adult lying wide awake under a quilt in a dim dorm room at dusk, with a packed suitcase by the door.
image.caption: The clock's evening wake signal before habitual bedtime can make it hard to fall asleep early.

hops.title: How REM sleep was almost called JEM sleep
hops.text: REM sleep was nearly called JEM sleep. In late 1951 the graduate student Eugene Aserinsky attached EEG and eye-movement electrodes to his own eight-year-old son and recorded him all night. From watching sleeping infants, he expected quiet stretches with no eye movement. Instead he found stretches of vigorous, darting eye movement lasting about twenty minutes. He first meant to call them "Jerky Eye Movement," or JEM, periods, then settled on REM. His advisor, Nathaniel Kleitman, played the skeptic and demanded airtight proof. The result cut against his own theory: REM sleep came with an active cortex, and Kleitman had held that sleep was entirely passive.

sources.citation: Aserinsky E, Journal of the History of the Neurosciences 5(3):213-227 (1996).

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A vintage chart recorder on a lamp-lit laboratory desk tracing wavy ink lines on a long paper roll.
image.caption: An all-night recording in 1951 turned up stretches of rapid eye movement during sleep, later named REM.

hops.afterHeading: The switch: why sleep comes in one block
hops.title: Why the older allergy pills make people drowsy
hops.text: Histamine sounds like a runny-nose problem, but the histamine neurons of the tuberomammillary nucleus are also one of the wake-promoting groups on the awake side of the switch. In PET scans, an oral dose of diphenhydramine, the older antihistamine in Benadryl, reached the brain and occupied about 56 percent of cortical H1 histamine receptors, and the drug is well known for causing drowsiness. In a separate scan study, fexofenadine, sold as Allegra, occupied essentially none, and volunteers rated themselves no sleepier than on placebo. Both are antihistamines; in these scans they differed sharply in how much they bound to histamine receptors in the brain.

sources.citation: MedlinePlus Drug Information: Diphenhydramine (a682539), U.S. National Library of Medicine.
MedlinePlus Drug Information: Fexofenadine (a697035), U.S. National Library of Medicine.
Tashiro M et al., British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology 65(6):811-821 (2008).
Tashiro M et al., Journal of Clinical Pharmacology 44(8):890-900 (2004).

audio.title: A wandering liver, a dropped cup and ducks on guard duty
audio.transcript:
Here are three true stories about sleep and biological time, each stranger than it has any right to be.

First, a liver that moved to a different time zone while the brain stayed home. In two thousand and one, researchers at the University of Virginia studied rats whose tissues carried a glowing clock reporter, which let the researchers track the clock by measuring the light given off by tissue samples. The room stayed on an ordinary cycle of light and dark, and the master clock in the brain, the S C N, stayed locked to that light. Then the researchers changed only one thing: when the rats could eat. Within two days of the new feeding schedule, the liver's rhythm had shifted by about ten hours, while the S C N kept time with the lights. The liver had followed the food, not the light. The S C N is the master clock, but it is not the only clock, and food can pull the others away from it. This was shown in rats on a fixed feeding schedule; whether one late meal does the same in a person, this study does not say.

Second, Paris, two thousand twenty-one, and a test of a story about Thomas Edison. Edison supposedly napped in a chair holding metal balls, so that as he dozed off they would clatter to the floor and wake him with a fresh idea. A team at the Paris Brain Institute gave one hundred and three volunteers a set of number problems with a hidden shortcut that nobody was told about. Then each volunteer rested in a dark room, holding a light plastic cup of about fifty-five grams that cost around three euros, while polysomnography recorded their E E G, eye movements and muscle tone. Leave aside the people who spotted the shortcut before the break. Of the rest, eighty-three percent of those who spent at least fifteen seconds in light stage N one, and went no deeper, found it afterward, against thirty-one percent of those scored as awake. The odd part is what happened one stage deeper. Of the fourteen volunteers who slipped into N two, the stage of sleep spindles and K-complexes, only two found the shortcut. For this number puzzle, the people who stopped at the edge of sleep were the most likely to spot the shortcut. The dropped cup itself turned out to be only a rough marker of where that edge was.

Third, sleeping with half a brain. In nineteen ninety-nine, researchers lined up mallard ducks in rows of four and recorded their brain waves and their eyes. Compared with the ducks in the middle, ducks at the exposed ends of the row showed a one hundred and fifty percent increase in the share of their slow-wave sleep spent with one half of the brain asleep and the other half awake. During that one-sided sleep one eye stays open, and the end ducks usually pointed that eye outward, away from the group. That open eye is wired to the awake half of the brain. When the researchers showed a threatening image to the open eye, the ducks reacted fast. The middle ducks, with neighbors on both sides, spent far less of their sleep half awake.

So a rat's liver can follow its meals instead of the light, a number puzzle went best for people who stopped at the edge of sleep, and a duck can keep half its brain on watch. A body clock can shift on its own, and the two sides of a duck's brain can sleep separately.
